Fix an integer $s\ge5$, a finite number $T>0$, the closed interval $J=[0,T]$, and the flat spatial torus $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$. Use the spaces $H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ and one fixed periodic symmetric-hyperbolic system as defined in [[def-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-system]]: its state domain $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is open, its coefficient maps $A^\mu(t,x,z),B(t,x,z)$ are smooth on the stated time, torus and state domain, each $A^\mu$ is symmetric, and $A^0$ is positive definite. The fixed-gauge Einstein state is the finite vector $z=(g_{ab},p_{ab},q_{abi},w)$, where $p_{ab}=\partial_0g_{ab}$, $q_{abi}=\partial_i g_{ab}$, and $w$ is the complete matter and auxiliary state of one fixed reduction.

For the SI interpretation, the system's time parameter $t$ is the length coordinate $x^0=ct_{\rm phys}$ in metres, while $x^i$ are dimensionless angular coordinates on the torus. The metric components then have coordinate-dependent units: $g_{00}$ is dimensionless, $g_{0i}$ has units of metres, and $g_{ij}$ has units of square metres. Accordingly $p_{ab}=\partial_0g_{ab}$ has units $[g_{ab}]\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $q_{abi}=\partial_i g_{ab}$ has units $[g_{ab}]$. The model-specific components of $w$ have the fixed units declared by that reduction. Divide each component by its fixed declared unit scale before forming the Euclidean-valued state and its Sobolev norm; the resulting numerical state is dimensionless. The coefficient and source fields are those of this same fixed normalized reduction. Thus $R_z$ is a bound on that normalized state, and $R_t$ is a separate bound on its derivative with respect to the length coordinate $x^0$ (units $\mathrm m^{-1}$). Neither is a unit-independent physical observable. If physical seconds are used instead, then $\partial_{x^0}=c^{-1}\partial_{t_{\rm phys}}$; consequently the term $A^0\partial_{x^0}$ becomes $c^{-1}A^0\partial_{t_{\rm phys}}$ unless the entire equation is multiplied by $c$.

A fixed-gauge finite-slab comparison context consists of one such coefficient family on an open time interval containing $J$, one coordinate gauge and reconstruction rule, compact state sets $K_0\subset\operatorname{int}K_1\subset\operatorname{int}K_2\subset O$, separate finite nonnegative bounds $R_z,R_t$, and constants $0<a\le b<\infty$ such that

$$a|\zeta|^2\le \zeta^{\mathsf T}A^0(t,x,z)\zeta\le b|\zeta|^2$$

for every $t\in J$, $x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $z\in K_2$, and $\zeta\in\mathbb R^m$. The reference state takes values in $K_0$. Compared classical states take values in $K_1$, belong to $L^\infty(J;H^s)\cap C^0(J;H^{s-1})$, have $\partial_tz\in L^\infty(J;H^{s-1})$, and satisfy
$$\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{t\in J}\|z(t)\|_{H^s}\le R_z,\qquad \operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{t\in J}\|\partial_tz(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le R_t.$$
The outer set $K_2$ supplies the positive coefficient margin for local existence restarted from data in compact subsets of $K_1$. Two states use the same chart grid, coefficient maps, gauge source functions, reconstruction rule, and fixed matter branch. Forcing terms, when included in a comparison, are continuous $H^{s-1}$-valued functions of the slab parameter; their size is controlled through the separate stated solution and time-derivative bounds when the comparison estimate is applied.

The Sobolev norms compare coordinate fields in this fixed gauge. They do not identify two arbitrary coordinate representatives by a diffeomorphism. The Einstein interpretation uses the same first-order reduction, full initial constraints, complete matter data, and local restart hypotheses throughout the finite slab.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Dependent Choice. Fix $s\ge5$, a finite slab $J=[0,T]$ with $T>0$, a smooth periodic symmetric-hyperbolic coefficient family on an open state set $O$, and a fixed-gauge comparison context with $K_0\subset\operatorname{int}K_1\subset\operatorname{int}K_2\subset O$, a uniform positive time-matrix bound on $K_2$, and the separate state and time-derivative bounds $R_z,R_t$ of [[def-gr-fx-fixed-gauge-data-topology]]. Let $u,v$ be classical solutions in that context with state range in $K_1$, each with its own source $F_u,F_v\in C(J;H^{s-1})$ in the reduced system

$$A^0(t,x,u)\partial_tu+\sum_{i=1}^3A^i(t,x,u)\partial_i u+B(t,x,u)=F_u,$$

and the analogous equation for $v$. Then there is a constant $C>0$, depending only on the fixed coefficient family, compact state sets, positive time-matrix margin, $R_z$, $R_t$, $s$, and $T$, such that for every $t\in[0,T]$

$$\|u(t)-v(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le C e^{Ct}\left(\|u(0)-v(0)\|_{H^{s-1}}+\int_0^t\|F_u(r)-F_v(r)\|_{H^{s-1}}\,dr\right),$$

In particular, when both sources vanish, the finite-slab estimate holds for two solutions of the same reduced system. Fix a smooth reference solution on $J$ with state range in $K_0$ and bounded $H^s$ norm. There is an $H^s$ neighborhood of its initial value such that every smooth, admissible datum in that neighborhood has a solution of the same unforced system on all of $J$, with state range in $K_1$ and a common finite $H^s$ bound. The neighborhood size and bound may depend on the chosen slab and reference solution.

For the geometric interpretation, specialize to a fixed harmonic-gauge reduction of one covariant Einstein-matter model satisfying the complete-data initialization, smooth reconstruction, auxiliary-constraint propagation, and matter-conservation hypotheses of [[thm-gr-local-geometric-development]]. Take the initial hypersurface to be $\Sigma=\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, fix $\kappa>0$, $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, a smooth Riemannian metric $h$ and smooth symmetric second fundamental form $K_{\rm ext}$, with $K_{\rm ext}(V,W)=g(\nabla_Vn,W)$ for the future unit normal. Let $\mathcal V=\mathbb RN\oplus T\Sigma$ be the abstract initial normal bundle with metric $g_0(aN+X,bN+Y)=-ab+h(X,Y)$, and let $T_0$ be the stress tensor computed from complete matter data $d$ on that bundle. Assume the initial state is the complete initialization of $(h,K_{\rm ext},d)$, the reconstructed metric remains time-oriented Lorentzian with every $t$-slice spacelike on $J$, and the initial harmonic gauge residual $H$ vanishes. Require the exact constraints

$$S_h+(\operatorname{tr}_hK_{\rm ext})^2-|K_{\rm ext}|_h^2=2\Lambda+2\kappa T_0(N,N),\qquad \operatorname{div}_hK_{\rm ext}-d\operatorname{tr}_hK_{\rm ext}=\kappa T_0(N,\cdot)$$

and every auxiliary compatibility condition hold. Assume the smooth reduced solution and its matter equations and conserved stress persist on $J$ under the same fixed reconstruction and branch. Then it reconstructs to a solution of the original Einstein-matter equations throughout the slab after the fixed-gauge identifications. For a pair of constrained data sets satisfying these hypotheses separately, this conclusion applies to each member of the pair. This is a mathematical model deduction conditional on those hypotheses; it asserts no uniform collar for noncompact initial surfaces.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold, let $g$ be a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor on $M$, and let $\Phi:M\to M$ be a smooth diffeomorphism. The pullback tensor $\Phi^*g$ is the smooth covariant $2$-tensor defined at each $p\in M$ by

$$(\Phi^*g)_p(X,Y):=g_{\Phi(p)}(d\Phi_pX,d\Phi_pY),\qquad X,Y\in T_pM.$$

When $g$ is Lorentzian, this formula defines the metric components seen in the coordinate representative obtained by $\Phi$. Equality of $\Phi^*g$ and $g$ means equality of the bilinear forms on each tangent space, not equality of their component arrays in a chosen chart.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $c>0$ be a fixed real constant.
All curves below take values in $M$; the physical reading of $c$, of a
worldline as the history of a clock or body, and of the parameter values as
times is not part of this definition and is adopted separately in the
postulates of the framework.

**(a) Regularity classes.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A
**chart representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ for a smooth
chart $(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]).

- For $k\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ and an interior point $t_0\in I$, the map
  $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ at $t_0$** when there is a chart representative
  $x\circ\gamma$ defined near $t_0$ that is $C^k$ there in the componentwise
  Euclidean sense. This condition is independent of the chart: on the overlap
  of two chart representatives the transition map is smooth and the chain rule
  applies ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]],
  [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). If $t_0\in I$ is an
  included endpoint of $I$, the coordinate representative and its derivatives through order $k$
  are continuous up to $t_0$ on the relative interval
  $I\cap(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$, with derivatives at
  $t_0$ taken one-sided. For $k=\infty$ this holds at every finite order.
  Merely possessing a one-sided secant tangent, as defined next, does not
  by itself make a curve $C^1$ at the endpoint. The map $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ on $I$** when it is $C^k$ at
  every point of $I$.

- Let $b\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. A curve
  $\gamma:(b-\varepsilon,b]\to M$ has **left tangent** $v\in T_{\gamma(b)}M$
  at $b$ when for one — equivalently every — chart $(U,x)$ around
  $\gamma(b)$, writing $v=\sum_{a=0}^{3}v^a\partial_a|_{\gamma(b)}$
  ([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the
  difference quotients satisfy
  $\bigl(x^a(\gamma(t))-x^a(\gamma(b))\bigr)/(t-b)\to v^a$ as $t\uparrow b$ for
  $a=0,1,2,3$. A **right tangent** at the left end of a curve is defined
  analogously with $t\downarrow b$. Chart independence is the one-sided
  chain-rule computation for the smooth transition maps
  ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

- A curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ is **piecewise $C^1$** when there is a
  finite partition $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ such that for every $i$ the
  restriction of $\gamma$ to $[s_{i-1},s_i]$ is $C^1$ up to its included
  endpoints in the one-sided sense above: in every endpoint chart its
  component derivatives on the open piece have continuous one-sided limits,
  agreeing with its endpoint derivatives. Equivalently each piece has a
  $C^1$ extension to its closed parameter piece. In particular its right
  tangent at $s_{i-1}$ and left tangent at $s_i$ exist. Such a
  partition is called **admissible** for $\gamma$. The piece extensions give continuity at the
  corners; no agreement of the
  two one-sided tangents at a corner is required.

**(b) Velocity.** If $\gamma$ is $C^1$ at an interior point $t$, its
**velocity** $\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation
$[f]\mapsto(f\circ\gamma)'(t)$ on smooth germs at $\gamma(t)$, extending
[[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]] from smooth to $C^1$ curves.
Equal germ representatives agree along the curve near $t$, and the
one-variable product rule proves the derivation identity. In a chart around
$\gamma(t)$ the velocity has the component
expression

$$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x^a\circ\gamma\bigr)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)},$$

the coordinate expression of the derivation
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). At an
included endpoint of the domain, $\gamma'$ means the corresponding one-sided
tangent of clause (a).

**(c) Timelike worldlines.** For $k\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$,
a **$C^k$ future timelike worldline** is a $C^k$
curve $\gamma:I\to M$ whose velocity $\gamma'(t)$ is future timelike at every
$t\in I$, in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]
and [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]: $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))<0$
and $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),N_{\gamma(t)})<0$. A **piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike worldline** is a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ whose
velocity at every point of each open piece and whose one-sided tangents at the
two ends of each piece are future timelike; the definition is applied to a map
on an arbitrary interval $I$ with nonempty interior by requiring it on every
compact subinterval of $I$. A future timelike velocity is in particular
nonzero, so every future timelike worldline is regular.

**(d) Proper time and length.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$
future timelike worldline and let $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ be an admissible
partition. On each open piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the function

$$h_i(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}\bigl(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s)\bigr)}$$

is continuous and strictly positive: it is a finite sum of products of
continuous real functions in any chart around a point of the piece, as
$g_{ab}\circ\gamma$ and the components of $\gamma'$ are continuous
([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and the
square root is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ ([[def-rational-power]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The continuous one-sided limits of the component derivatives, required
by the $C^1$ extension of each piece, and continuity of $g$ imply that
$h_i$ tends to the norm of the corresponding endpoint tangent. The future
timelike hypothesis on those tangents makes these limits strictly positive, and $h_i$ extends to a continuous function on
$[s_{i-1},s_i]$; hence it is Darboux integrable there
([[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). The
**proper-time increment** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is

$$\tau(b)-\tau(a):=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}h_i(s)\,ds,$$

and the **Lorentzian length** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is
$L_g(\gamma):=c\,(\tau(b)-\tau(a))$. For a base point $s_0\in I$ the
**proper-time function** $\tau:I\to\mathbb R$ of a future timelike worldline is
the function with $\tau(s_0)=0$ and $\tau(s)$ equal to the increment
from $s_0$ to $s$ when $s>s_0$, and minus the increment from $s$ to $s_0$
when $s<s_0$. That the increment is independent of the admissible
partition, so that $\tau$ is well defined, and that it is invariant under
increasing $C^1$ reparametrization with strictly positive derivative
(including one-sided endpoint derivatives), comparing the increment over the
actual image interval, are proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]; the display is the
value for any admissible partition.

**(e) Four-velocity.** Let $\gamma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike
worldline and let $t$ be a parameter value at which $\gamma$ is differentiable
(interior point of a piece, or an included endpoint with its one-sided
tangent). The **four-velocity** of $\gamma$ at $t$ is

$$U(t):=\frac{c\,\gamma'(t)}{\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M .$$

By construction $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$, and
$\gamma'(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}/c\bigr)U(t)$ with a strictly
positive scalar factor. If $U$ is written as the derivative of $\gamma$ with
respect to proper time, $U=d\gamma/d\tau$, this is a statement proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]], not part of the
present definition.

**(f) Scope.** Proper time, length and four-velocity are defined only for
future timelike worldlines. A null or spacelike curve receives no proper time
and no four-velocity from this definition, and no limiting or distributional
extension of the square-root integrand to such curves is asserted. The
parametrization of a worldline is part of the data and is arbitrary in this
definition: no affine parameter, no geodesic equation, no completeness or
extendability of the domain, and no measurement or clock reading is assumed.
Null and spacelike regularity classes are not defined here beyond the general
$C^k$ and piecewise-$C^1$ notions of clause (a), which make no causal
requirement.

Let $s\ge5$ be an integer and let $J=[0,T]$, $T>0$, be a compact slab for one unforced smooth symmetric-hyperbolic reduction and the fixed gauge of [[def-gr-fx-fixed-gauge-data-topology]]. Let $z_n,z$ be classical solutions with the same coefficient family, gauge, matter branch and reconstruction rule. Assume their states lie in one compact admissible set, their $H^s$ and time-derivative norms have a common finite bound, and their initial data converge in $H^{s-1}$. Take $g_n,g$ to be the $g_{ab}$ components of those first-order states in the common coordinates. Then $g_n\to g$ in $C^1(J\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi})$.

Fix a compact parameter interval $I=[a,b]$, a common coordinate chart $U$ with closure in $(0,T)\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and a compact subset $K$ of its position-velocity phase space. If future timelike geodesics $\gamma_n:I\to M$ of $g_n$ have initial position-velocity data converging to those of a $g$-geodesic $\gamma$, and all the position-velocity lifts, including that of $\gamma$, stay in $K$, then $\gamma_n\to\gamma$ in $C^1(I)$ in chart components.

Finally, assume the curves are future timelike for their respective metrics, share the fixed time orientation and constant $c>0$ of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]], and have a uniform timelike margin
$$g_n(\dot\gamma_n(\lambda),\dot\gamma_n(\lambda))\le-\eta<0\qquad(n\ge1,\ \lambda\in I).$$
Then their proper times converge:
$$\frac1c\int_a^b\sqrt{-g_n(\dot\gamma_n,\dot\gamma_n)}\,d\lambda\longrightarrow\frac1c\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)}\,d\lambda.$$
All conclusions concern a fixed finite slab and a fixed coordinate gauge; they assert no uniformity as $T\to\infty$ and no identification of arbitrary coordinate representatives.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length,

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds. A **diffeomorphism** from $M$ to $N$ is a
bijective smooth map $F:M\to N$ whose inverse $F^{-1}:N\to M$ is smooth. Since
a bijective smooth map and its smooth inverse are both continuous
([[prop-smooth-maps-are-continuous]]), every diffeomorphism is a homeomorphism,
but the converse fails. The manifolds $M$ and $N$ are **diffeomorphic**, written
$M\cong N$, when a diffeomorphism $M\to N$ exists.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map. Then $F$ is a **local diffeomorphism** when
every $p\in M$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq M$ such that $F(U)$ is
open in $N$ and the corestriction $F|_{U}^{F(U)}:U\to F(U)$ is a
diffeomorphism onto the open submanifold $F(U)$
([[prop-an-open-subset-of-a-smooth-manifold-has-a-canonical-restricted-smooth-structure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) for the quotient, product-measure and integration
clauses below, as in [[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]].

**(a) The 2 pi-periodic torus.** Let $\mathbb T_{2\pi}:=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$
carry the quotient topology, and let
$$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}:=\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}\times\mathbb T_{2\pi}$$
with the product topology; write $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ for the
quotient map and $[x]:=(x^1+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^2+2\pi\mathbb Z,x^3+2\pi\mathbb Z)$.
The map $[0,2\pi)^3\to\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $x\mapsto[x]$, is a bijection. The
normalized product measure $\mu$ is $\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}\otimes\mu_{\mathbb T}$,
where $\mu_{\mathbb T}$ is the normalized measure of
[[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]] transported by
$t\mapsto2\pi t$; it is a probability measure on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ and $\int f\,d\mu=(2\pi)^{-3}\int_{[0,2\pi)^3}f\circ q\,d\lambda_3$
for bounded measurable $f$ ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

**(b) Test functions and continuous classes.** For $N\ge1$ let
$C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the set of maps
$u:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb R^N$ whose pullbacks
$\widetilde u:=u\circ q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$ are smooth;
these are the **smooth test functions** (real-valued when $N=1$).
Equivalently every smooth map $\widetilde u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^N$
that is $2\pi$-periodic in each coordinate descends to the unique map
$u([x])=\widetilde u(x)$, since periodicity makes this value independent of
$x$ in its equivalence class. For an integer $m\ge0$, define
$C^m(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ similarly by requiring
$\widetilde u\in C^m(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^N)$
([[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]), and define
$D^\alpha u([x]):=D^\alpha\widetilde u(x)$ for $|\alpha|\le m$.
Derivatives of a periodic $C^m$ map are periodic, so these values are
well-defined, with
$$\|u\|_{C^m}:=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\ \sup_{x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}|(D^\alpha u)(x)|,$$
where the multi-index derivative is that of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]].

**(c) The Hilbert space $L^2$.** For $N\ge1$ let
$L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ be the quotient of the set of measurable
$u$ with $\int|u|^2\,d\mu<\infty$ by the $\mu$-a.e. zero functions
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]),
with inner product $\langle u,v\rangle_2=\int u\cdot v\,d\mu$ and norm
$\|u\|_2=\langle u,u\rangle_2^{1/2}$; it is a real Hilbert space
([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]). For
$u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)$ and $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ the
**$k$-th Fourier coefficient** is the vector
$$\widehat u(k):=\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u(x)\,e^{-ik\cdot x}\,d\mu(x)\in\mathbb C^N ,$$
where $e^{-ik\cdot x}:=\chi_{-k}$ with $\chi_k([x]):=\exp(i\,k\cdot x)$; here
$u$ is read through any representative. Write $\chi_k:\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb C$,
$k\in\mathbb Z^3$, for these **characters**; under the identification
$x=2\pi y$ they are the characters $\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot y)$ of
[[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]], so $(\chi_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}$
is an orthonormal basis of the complex space $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb C)$.

**(d) Weak derivatives and the periodic Sobolev spaces.** For
$u,v\in L^1(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ say that
$v$ is the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_{\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}}v\,\varphi\,d\mu$$
for every $\varphi\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R)$, where $D^\alpha\varphi$
is the multi-index derivative of the periodic representative
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]] records the
Euclidean analogue). For an integer $s\ge0$ let
$$H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):=\Bigl\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N):\ \text{for every }|\alpha|\le s\text{ there is }v_\alpha\in L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^N)\text{ with }v_\alpha=D^\alpha u\Bigr\},$$
the vector-valued weak derivative being componentwise, and put
$$\|u\|_{H^s}:=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le s}\|D^\alpha u\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.$$
The classes $L^2\subseteq L^1$ on the probability space, so the integrals in the
test identity are finite: $|\int u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,d\mu|\le\|u\|_2\|D^\alpha\varphi\|_2$
by Cauchy--Schwarz. The definition asserts neither that the weak derivative
exists nor that the two norms compared in the next item are equivalent; those
are proved in [[lem-gr-periodic-fourier-differentiation-and-norm-equivalence]].

**(e) Conventions.** $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ open, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an
interval and maps $F:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^{m'}$ are
called smooth when the representative $G(t,x,u):=F(t,q(x),u)$ is
locally the restriction of a smooth Euclidean map: for every
$(t,x,u)\in I\times\mathbb R^3\times O$ there are an open neighborhood
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^{4+m}$ and $\widetilde G\in C^\infty(V;\mathbb R^{m'})$
with $\widetilde G=G$ on $V\cap(I\times\mathbb R^3\times O)$.
For open $I$ this is the ordinary Euclidean definition. For nonopen $I$
it is the local extension convention at included endpoints, also admitting
a singleton interval. On a nondegenerate interval endpoint time derivatives
are the limits of interior derivatives; on a singleton no time derivative
is specified without choosing an extension. Throughout this page the torus is always this
$2\pi$-periodic one; a statement "for every $x$" means for every point of
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and "a.e." means $\mu$-a.e.

derivations.claim: Lift the circle map to $F_\epsilon(x)=x+\epsilon\sin x$ on $\mathbb R$. By [F8], repeated differentiation makes $\sin$ smooth, and its first derivative gives $F_\epsilon'(x)=1+\epsilon\cos x\ge1-|\epsilon|>0$. The mean-value theorem [F11] makes $F_\epsilon$ strictly increasing. Periodicity [F9] gives $F_\epsilon(x+2\pi)=F_\epsilon(x)+2\pi$, and boundedness [F10] gives $F_\epsilon(x)-x$ bounded; hence its limits at the two ends of $\mathbb R$ are $\pm\infty$. For any real target, choose endpoints with the target between their images and apply [F12]; strict increase gives uniqueness of the preimage. Thus $F_\epsilon$ is bijective. Its derivative never vanishes, so [F4] makes the inverse smooth locally at every point, hence globally smooth. The translation identity makes the map and inverse descend to smooth inverse maps on the circle in [F14]; extending by the identity in the other coordinates gives a bijective smooth map with smooth inverse, hence the diffeomorphism $\Phi_\epsilon$ by [F13].

In these coordinates $d\Phi_\epsilon$ is diagonal with entries $1$, $1+\epsilon\cos x^1$, $1$, $1$. Applying [F3] to the diagonal bilinear form gives $$(\Phi_\epsilon^*g)=-(dx^0)^2+L^2\bigl((1+\epsilon\cos x^1)^2(dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2\bigr).$$ At $x^1=0$, $(1+\epsilon)^2\ne1$ because $0<|\epsilon|<1$, so the component arrays differ. Since $1+\epsilon\cos x^1\ge1-|\epsilon|>0$, the displayed diagonal matrix has one negative and three positive entries and is Lorentzian by [F5].

The curve $\gamma(\lambda)=(\lambda,x_*)$ has tangent $\partial_0$ and is future timelike for $g$ with $g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=-1$. Since $\Phi_\epsilon$ fixes $x^0$ and acts only on spatial coordinates, $\Phi_\epsilon\circ\gamma$ is also a unit-coordinate-time axis and $g((\Phi_\epsilon\circ\gamma)',(\Phi_\epsilon\circ\gamma)')=-1$. By [F3], $(\Phi_\epsilon^*g)(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=g((\Phi_\epsilon\circ\gamma)',(\Phi_\epsilon\circ\gamma)')=-1$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix an integer $m\ge1$, an open set
$O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ with the subspace topology and a nondegenerate open
interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ containing $0$. All functions on
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ are those of [[def-gr-periodic-torus-and-sobolev-spaces]],
and smoothness on $I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O$ means smoothness of the
representative in the sense of clause (e) of that item.

**(a) Coefficients.** A **periodic symmetric hyperbolic coefficient family** on
$O$ consists of smooth maps
$$A^\mu:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\operatorname{Sym}_m(\mathbb R)\quad(\mu=0,1,2,3),\qquad B:I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O\to\mathbb R^m,$$
such that $A^0(t,x,u)$ is positive definite for every
$(t,x,u)\in I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\times O$; here
$\operatorname{Sym}_m(\mathbb R)$ is the real vector space of symmetric
$m\times m$ matrices, identified with symmetric endomorphisms of $\mathbb R^m$
through the standard coordinate inner product, and positive definiteness means
$z^TA^0(t,x,u)z>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^m$
([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]).

**(b) The system.** The associated **symmetric hyperbolic system** is
$$A^0(t,x,u)\,\partial_tu+\sum_{i=1}^3A^i(t,x,u)\,\partial_iu+B(t,x,u)=0 .\qquad(\star)$$

**(c) Values and norms.** For each integer $s\ge0$, an $H^s$ class
$u\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ **takes values in a set
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$** when it has a continuous representative whose values
lie in $E$. Such a representative is unique, since continuous functions equal
almost everywhere on the torus agree everywhere. A map $u:J\to H^s$ with
$J\subseteq I$ takes values in $E$ when every class $u(t)$ does. For compact
$K\subseteq O$ and $R\ge0$ put
$$\mathcal S_s(K,R):=\bigl\{u_0\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m):u_0\text{ takes values in }K,\ \|u_0\|_{H^s}\le R\bigr\}.$$
When an item fixes $s$, it may abbreviate this class by $\mathcal S(K,R)$.

**(d) Classical solutions.** Let $s\ge2$ be an integer and let $J\subseteq I$ be
an interval. A **classical solution of $(\star)$ on
$J\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$** is a $C^1$ map
$u:J\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}\to\mathbb R^m$ with $u(t,x)\in O$ for all
$(t,x)$ and $(\star)$ satisfied at every point, such that
$u\in L^\infty(J;H^s)$ and $\partial_tu\in L^\infty(J;H^{s-1})$.

**(e) Sobolev solutions.** Let $s\ge5$ be an integer and let $J\subseteq I$ be
an open interval. A map
$u:J\to H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ is a **Sobolev solution of
$(\star)$ on $J$** when

1. $u\in L^\infty(J;H^s)\cap C^0(J;H^{s-1})$ and the distributional time
   derivative $\partial_tu$ lies in $L^\infty(J;H^{s-1})$;
2. $u$ takes values in $O$ using the continuous representatives from (c);
3. for almost every $t\in J$ the identity $(\star)$ holds in
   $L^2(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$, with coefficients evaluated using
   the continuous representative of $u(t)$. This condition requires each
   displayed product to define an $L^2$ class; it does not assert a global
   coefficient-composition bound depending only on $\|u(t)\|_{H^s}$.

**(f) Initial data.** For an integer $s\ge5$, **initial data for $(\star)$ at
time $0$** are a class $u_0\in H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ whose values
lie in a compact subset of $O$; a solution **has initial value $u_0$** when
$u(t)\to u_0$ in $H^{s-1}$ as $t\to0$ within $J$.

The definition introduces the system and its solution classes only; existence,
uniqueness, continuous dependence and smooth persistence are asserted and
proved in [[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-existence]],
[[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-uniqueness-stability]] and
[[thm-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-smooth-persistence]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$, there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$. Induction (The principle of mathematical induction): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ (The von Neumann naturals form a Peano system) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
(Zero and one under multiplication) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
(Cancellation for multiplication by a nonzero factor). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ (Addition is cancellative). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
(Multiplication is associative, Multiplication is commutative) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional (Multiplication of natural numbers), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in Field, and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Dependent Choice. Fix $s\ge5$, a finite slab $J=[0,T]$ with $T>0$, a smooth periodic symmetric-hyperbolic coefficient family on an open state set $O$, and a fixed-gauge comparison context with $K_0\subset\operatorname{int}K_1\subset\operatorname{int}K_2\subset O$, a uniform positive time-matrix bound on $K_2$, and the separate state and time-derivative bounds $R_z,R_t$ of [[def-gr-fx-fixed-gauge-data-topology]]. Let $u,v$ be classical solutions in that context with state range in $K_1$, each with its own source $F_u,F_v\in C(J;H^{s-1})$ in the reduced system

$$A^0(t,x,u)\partial_tu+\sum_{i=1}^3A^i(t,x,u)\partial_i u+B(t,x,u)=F_u,$$

and the analogous equation for $v$. Then there is a constant $C>0$, depending only on the fixed coefficient family, compact state sets, positive time-matrix margin, $R_z$, $R_t$, $s$, and $T$, such that for every $t\in[0,T]$

$$\|u(t)-v(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le C e^{Ct}\left(\|u(0)-v(0)\|_{H^{s-1}}+\int_0^t\|F_u(r)-F_v(r)\|_{H^{s-1}}\,dr\right),$$

In particular, when both sources vanish, the finite-slab estimate holds for two solutions of the same reduced system. Fix a smooth reference solution on $J$ with state range in $K_0$ and bounded $H^s$ norm. There is an $H^s$ neighborhood of its initial value such that every smooth, admissible datum in that neighborhood has a solution of the same unforced system on all of $J$, with state range in $K_1$ and a common finite $H^s$ bound. The neighborhood size and bound may depend on the chosen slab and reference solution.

For the geometric interpretation, specialize to a fixed harmonic-gauge reduction of one covariant Einstein-matter model satisfying the complete-data initialization, smooth reconstruction, auxiliary-constraint propagation, and matter-conservation hypotheses of [[thm-gr-local-geometric-development]]. Take the initial hypersurface to be $\Sigma=\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, fix $\kappa>0$, $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, a smooth Riemannian metric $h$ and smooth symmetric second fundamental form $K_{\rm ext}$, with $K_{\rm ext}(V,W)=g(\nabla_Vn,W)$ for the future unit normal. Let $\mathcal V=\mathbb RN\oplus T\Sigma$ be the abstract initial normal bundle with metric $g_0(aN+X,bN+Y)=-ab+h(X,Y)$, and let $T_0$ be the stress tensor computed from complete matter data $d$ on that bundle. Assume the initial state is the complete initialization of $(h,K_{\rm ext},d)$, the reconstructed metric remains time-oriented Lorentzian with every $t$-slice spacelike on $J$, and the initial harmonic gauge residual $H$ vanishes. Require the exact constraints

$$S_h+(\operatorname{tr}_hK_{\rm ext})^2-|K_{\rm ext}|_h^2=2\Lambda+2\kappa T_0(N,N),\qquad \operatorname{div}_hK_{\rm ext}-d\operatorname{tr}_hK_{\rm ext}=\kappa T_0(N,\cdot)$$

and every auxiliary compatibility condition hold. Assume the smooth reduced solution and its matter equations and conserved stress persist on $J$ under the same fixed reconstruction and branch. Then it reconstructs to a solution of the original Einstein-matter equations throughout the slab after the fixed-gauge identifications. For a pair of constrained data sets satisfying these hypotheses separately, this conclusion applies to each member of the pair. This is a mathematical model deduction conditional on those hypotheses; it asserts no uniform collar for noncompact initial surfaces.

Let $s\ge5$ be an integer and let $J=[0,T]$, $T>0$, be a compact slab for one unforced smooth symmetric-hyperbolic reduction and the fixed gauge of [[def-gr-fx-fixed-gauge-data-topology]]. Let $z_n,z$ be classical solutions with the same coefficient family, gauge, matter branch and reconstruction rule. Assume their states lie in one compact admissible set, their $H^s$ and time-derivative norms have a common finite bound, and their initial data converge in $H^{s-1}$. Take $g_n,g$ to be the $g_{ab}$ components of those first-order states in the common coordinates. Then $g_n\to g$ in $C^1(J\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi})$.

Fix a compact parameter interval $I=[a,b]$, a common coordinate chart $U$ with closure in $(0,T)\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, and a compact subset $K$ of its position-velocity phase space. If future timelike geodesics $\gamma_n:I\to M$ of $g_n$ have initial position-velocity data converging to those of a $g$-geodesic $\gamma$, and all the position-velocity lifts, including that of $\gamma$, stay in $K$, then $\gamma_n\to\gamma$ in $C^1(I)$ in chart components.

Finally, assume the curves are future timelike for their respective metrics, share the fixed time orientation and constant $c>0$ of [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]], and have a uniform timelike margin
$$g_n(\dot\gamma_n(\lambda),\dot\gamma_n(\lambda))\le-\eta<0\qquad(n\ge1,\ \lambda\in I).$$
Then their proper times converge:
$$\frac1c\int_a^b\sqrt{-g_n(\dot\gamma_n,\dot\gamma_n)}\,d\lambda\longrightarrow\frac1c\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)}\,d\lambda.$$
All conclusions concern a fixed finite slab and a fixed coordinate gauge; they assert no uniformity as $T\to\infty$ and no identification of arbitrary coordinate representatives.

derivations.claim: The coefficients in the Statement are smooth in $(t,x,z)$, each $A^\mu$ is symmetric, and $A^0=1$ is strictly positive. Thus [F1] makes this a symmetric-hyperbolic system. Its equation reduces to $\partial_tz=2tz$ and contains no spatial derivatives.

By [F3] and the chain rule, $z_\delta(t,x)=\delta\exp(t^2)$ satisfies $\partial_tz_\delta=2t\delta\exp(t^2)=2tz_\delta$ and $z_\delta(0,x)=\delta$. The zero solution corresponds to $\delta=0$. For each finite $T$, the function $\delta\exp(t^2)$ and its time derivative are bounded on $[0,T]$; its values lie between the endpoint values $\delta$ and $\delta\exp(T^2)$, hence in a compact interval. Since it is spatially constant, it has finite $H^s$ norm for every integer $s$. Its state and time-derivative bounds may depend on the selected finite $T$, as permitted by the finite-slab estimate [F5].

The difference from zero is exactly $\delta\exp(t^2)$. Homogeneity of the Sobolev norm on the spatially constant profile gives $$\frac{\|z_\delta(T)-z_0(T)\|_{H^{s-1}}}{\|z_\delta(0)-z_0(0)\|_{H^{s-1}}}=\frac{|\delta|\exp(T^2)\|\mathbf1\|_{H^{s-1}}}{|\delta|\|\mathbf1\|_{H^{s-1}}}=\exp(T^2).$$ Suppose one constant $C>0$ worked for all slab lengths in the displayed exponential estimate. Choose $T$ large enough that $y:=T^2-CT>C$. Then $y>0$, and [F2] gives $\exp(y)\ge1+y>C$. By [F4], $$\exp(T^2)=\exp(CT+y)=\exp(CT)\exp(y)>C\exp(CT),$$ since [F2] also gives $\exp(CT)>0$. This contradicts that uniform estimate.

For each fixed $T$, the exact solution map is multiplication by $\exp(t^2)$ and is Lipschitz on $[0,T]$ with finite constant $\exp(T^2)$; this is consistent with [F5] and [F6], whose constants and conclusions are attached to a fixed finite slab. The calculation establishes only that finite-slab continuity alone does not supply a $T$-independent exponential constant for general symmetric-hyperbolic systems.
